name: Adam Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brightwell Energy, a small firm of six that fits solar panels, home batteries and car chargers on houses. Most days I'm on a roof or in a garage by eight, running cable from the inverter to the fuse board. An inverter is the box that turns the panels' power into normal household power. Then I commission the system, which means switching it on, testing it and showing the owner the app.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it feels like the right side of history, people cutting their bills and their carbon. What wears me out is lofts in summer, and customers who've watched one video and think they know better than the regulations. I live with my girlfriend Priya, she's a nurse on nights half the month, so I cook a lot and we pass each other on the stairs. I use ChatGPT now and then to double-check a cable size or write a polite email to a difficult customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can get back to the real revolution, which is energy, not chatbots. At work we'd joke about it over lunch. Online I'd probably post something about how the money should have gone into insulation and heat pumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my work carries on as it is. Solar and chargers are growing, there's a few firms hiring in the area, and I've got about four months saved. The only thing on my mind is that the government grant for home batteries ends next year and orders might dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, same job, same van. I'd keep using the chatbot for the odd email, because it does save me twenty minutes. And I'd keep putting 150 a month aside, which is what we already do for a flat deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, if I'm honest. A bit annoyed at the wasted hype, but my work and money feel steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at Brightwell if the battery grant ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave, the owner, says we'd do more chargers and more repair work on older systems to fill the gap. He's been through one grant ending before and nobody lost their job. I trust him on that, he's straight with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're saving for a deposit. How close are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two years off, if Priya gets her band upgrade at the hospital. We look at flats on a Sunday morning like other people do crosswords. It's a nice dream to have while the work keeps coming.

say: I'd say the real change is **clean energy**, and the AI money should go to **insulation**.
At work we'd **joke about the hype** over lunch and carry on.
think: My solar and charger work keeps **growing**, and I have about **four months** saved.
The only worry is the **battery grant** ending next year and orders dipping.
do: Keep fitting **solar and chargers** at Brightwell as now.
Keep using a **chatbot** for the odd customer email to save time.
Keep saving **150 a month** toward a flat deposit with Priya.
feel: **Calm** about his work, with mild **annoyance** at the wasted hype.
S0.quote: We look at flats on a Sunday morning like other people do crosswords.
fieldNote: Sees his trade as part of a **bigger change** that matters more than AI.
Trusts his boss Dave, who has **steered through** a grant ending before.
A **secure, growing niche** plus four months saved makes calm believable here.

steps.text: Keep fitting solar panels and car chargers at Brightwell
Keep using a chatbot to draft difficult customer emails
Keep saving 150 a month toward a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance if we share the gains, like a shorter week for everyone instead of layoffs. At work I'd be the one saying let's try the new quoting tool before we judge it. Online I'd back calls for a tax on big tech profits to pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job looks fine, it's the office side of Brightwell that changes. Kerry does the quotes, the grid paperwork and the bookings, and all of that is exactly what this AI would do. I'd worry for Kerry, and I'd worry Dave would expect me to do more of the admin from the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once two or three other firms were using an AI design tool for panel layouts, I'd learn it, probably on a course Dave pays for. I'd keep working the same hours on the tools. And I'd join the electricians' union, which I keep meaning to do, so we've got a voice if things shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than worried. My hands are safe, but it's on my mind because the people around me aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a shorter week instead of layoffs. Do you think Dave would go for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave might, he's decent, but the bigger firms won't. The firms that do council contracts would cut the office and pocket the difference. That's why the union matters to me in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kerry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kerry to learn the grid paperwork rules inside out, because the AI will get them wrong sometimes and someone has to catch it. And I'd say come to the pub on Friday, we'll work it out. Kerry's been at Brightwell longer than me.

say: I'd argue for a **shorter week** for everyone rather than **layoffs**.
Online I'd back a **tax on tech profits** to pay for retraining.
think: My **hands-on work** is safe, but the **office side** of Brightwell shrinks.
I'd worry about **Kerry** and about doing more **admin** from the van.
do: Learn the **AI panel-layout tool** once other firms use it, on a paid course.
Join the **electricians' union** to have a voice as things shift.
Keep the same **hours on the tools** at Brightwell.
feel: **Uneasy**: his own job is safe, but colleagues' jobs are not.
S1.quote: The firms that do council contracts would cut the office and pocket the difference.
fieldNote: Classic steady adopter: he'll learn the tool **once others prove it**.
His worry is aimed at **Kerry in the office**, whose tasks match the card.
Blames **bigger firms and shareholders**, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Take a Dave-paid course on the AI panel-layout tool
Join the electricians' union this year
Keep working the same hours on solar installs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a plan from government, fast, like what they'd do in a war. Wage support, retraining, a slow-down on robots in homes until the safety rules exist. I'd be on the union's side at every meeting and I'd say so online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking part of my job goes in 2028: the system design, the quotes, the grid applications. That leaves me as the guy who carries panels up a ladder, and by 2031 a robot does that too. I'd be 31, which is young, but I'd have spent ten years on a trade that ends in five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd keep working hard while there's still work, and save more, maybe 300 a month by cutting our holiday. I'd learn to run and repair the robots and the AI design systems, because someone has to service them in the first years. And I'd sit down with Priya to rethink the flat, maybe wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel I have some control, but it's a real knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to service the robots. Do you really think that's you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, maybe. Electricians know wiring and safety, and those robots will need both. Servicing the robots is a bridge, not a career, and it would last until the robots fix each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Priya say about putting the flat off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would say her ward will still need nurses, so one of us is safe. And she'd be right, probably, but I don't want to be the one being carried. I'd rather wait on the flat than buy one we can only afford on her wage.

say: I'd say government needs a **wartime-style plan** with wage support and **retraining**.
I'd back a **slow-down on home robots** until safety rules exist.
think: The **design and quoting** half of my job goes in **2028**.
By **2031** robots carry the panels, after ten years in a **trade that ends**.
do: Save **300 a month** by cutting this year's **holiday**.
Learn to **service robots** and AI design systems as a bridge.
Put the **flat purchase** on hold with Priya.
feel: **Anxious**, with a **knot** in his stomach but some sense of control.
S2.quote: Servicing the robots is a bridge, not a career, and it would last until the robots fix each other.
fieldNote: He splits his job clearly into **thinking work** that goes first and **hands-on** later.
Priya's **nursing job** is his household's anchor, which he finds hard to accept.
Pride shows: he doesn't want to be **carried** on his partner's wage.

steps.text: Cut this year's holiday to save 300 a month
Learn to service robots and AI solar design systems
Put off buying a flat with Priya
Back union calls for wage support and home robot rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd push the union and the industry body to plan the transition together. I'd say it calmly, because panic never helped anyone up a ladder. Online I'd share anything practical, courses, grants, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years changes a lot for me. The design and paperwork go in 2031, the hands-on goes around 2034, when I'm 35. That's enough time to move into something nearby, like grid connection work or managing installs, if I start in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep fitting panels and add the AI design tool once it's common. I'd start a part-time course in energy systems, one evening a week. And I'd keep saving, but we'd probably still buy a small flat, just with a shorter mortgage term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a manageable kind. Five years feels more like a deadline than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why grid connection work? What's different about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big substations and the grid are messy, old, and every site is different. I reckon robots get there last. And it's still energy, which is the bit of my job I actually care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and stay put as an installer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw robots struggling with real lofts, which they might, lofts are chaos. If after three years the robots are still in showrooms, I'd stay and save the course money. I'm not going to jump just because a forecast says so.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so unions and industry should **plan together**.
I'd share practical things online, like **courses and grants**, not panic.
think: Hands-on work goes around **2034**, when I'm 35, which leaves time to move.
**Grid connection** work looks like the safest nearby step for me.
do: Add the **AI design tool** once it's common in the trade.
Start a **part-time energy course**, one evening a week.
Buy a **small flat** with a shorter mortgage term.
feel: **Anxious** in a manageable way, more **deadline** than cliff.
S3.quote: Five years feels more like a deadline than a cliff.
fieldNote: The extra time lets him **keep the flat plan** while he prepares.
He wants proof: he'll **watch robots** in real lofts before he jumps.
His loyalty is to **energy work**, not to installing as such.

steps.text: Start using the AI solar design tool once it's common
Take a part-time evening course in energy systems
Buy a small flat on a shorter mortgage term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it arguing. I'd want the union pushing for paid retraining time for everyone. At work I'd say let's keep our heads and keep fitting panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years and then three more for the robots takes me to 40. That's half a career. I'd likely be fine if I move toward grid work or design over the decade, and Priya's job will still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep installing, buy the flat on our normal plan, and learn the AI tools when the firm brings them in. Maybe in year three or four I'd start the energy course. Nothing dramatic in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly okay. It's far enough off to plan for properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice starting at Brightwell next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the apprentice to learn the electrics properly but also learn the software side, the monitoring apps and the grid rules. Don't just be hands. In ten years the hands alone won't be enough for an electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with the money, given a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably put a bit into a pension, which I never think about at 27. Priya keeps telling me to. If the robots come in 2039, I'd want something growing that isn't just my labour.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift, and the union should win **paid retraining** time.
At work I'd tell people to **keep their heads** and keep fitting panels.
think: Robots in **2039** take me to about **40**, half a career away.
Moving toward **grid or design work** over the decade should keep me fine.
do: Buy the **flat** on the normal plan with Priya.
Start a **pension** alongside the deposit savings.
Learn **AI tools** when Brightwell brings them in.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of his mind, but mostly settled.
S4.quote: In ten years the hands alone won't be enough for an electrician.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **keep normal life plans**, including the flat.
Thinks about a **pension** for the first time as a hedge against robots.
His advice to apprentices shows his real view: **hands plus software**.

steps.text: Keep installing panels and chargers at Brightwell
Buy a flat with Priya on the normal timeline
Start paying into a pension this year
Learn the firm's AI tools when they arrive

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the design side of my job would go almost at once and the robots right after. What would help is a proper public plan: wage support while people retrain, paid for by the companies making money from it. And a union with teeth, which means I need to actually join.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the climate side. If robots can fit panels cheaply, every roof gets solar, and part of me would be glad about that even while it costs me. I can hold both of those at once.

headlineQuote: If robots can fit panels cheaply, every roof gets solar, and part of me would be glad about that even while it costs me.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old solar installer** who also fits car chargers at a six-person firm.
He cares about **clean energy** and sees his trade as part of that cause.
He adopts tools **once others prove them**, and uses a chatbot now and then.
The **2028 scenario** makes him anxious because design work goes at once.
With more time he plans a **move toward grid work** and keeps the flat plan with Priya.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the design half of his job goes almost at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **public plan** with wage support during retraining, paid by **companies profiting**.
A **union with teeth**, which he intends to join.
